paragraphs.source_en:
Byron’s second letter on Bowles’s treatment of Pope, which was sent to John Murray in
April 1821 but not published until 1832 (Byron Prose 161–83, 459–91). In the second
letter Byron defends Eloisa to Abelard against the charge of ‘gross licentiousness’, express-
ing the highest esteem for the poem’s truthful representation of passion and delicacy of
style (Byron Prose 177–8). S.’s reading of Pope in May 1821 would also appear to have
been part of his preparation for Adonais (see headnote ‘Composition’) which was largely
composed between mid-May and mid-June. An Essay on Criticism is recalled in Adonais
101–4 (see note). So the presence of Pope in S.’s reading, correspondence and (no doubt)
conversation in the period from early May to August 1821 constitutes circumstantial evi-
dence for dating When passion’s trance within that period, though such evidence does not
warrant a decisive conclusion.
